## Does Ivermectin Lower COVID-19 Mortality? The Evidence

Your sister's belief reflects an early-pandemic hope that hasn't held up against rigorous, large-scale testing.

**Early "promising" studies were flawed.** Initial claims of ivermectin's benefit came largely from small, low-quality, or observational studies—some later retracted for data problems, including outright fraud (https://retractionwatch.com/2021/11/02/ivermectin-covid-19-study-retracted-authors-blame-file-mixup/). Early meta-analyses pooling these studies suggested a mortality benefit, but researchers cautioned this was "preliminary" and needed confirmation from large, well-designed trials (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43440-021-00245-z).

**Large, high-quality randomized trials found no benefit.** The definitive evidence comes from two major, well-conducted randomized controlled trials:
- The **TOGETHER trial** (NEJM, 2022), a large Brazilian outpatient study, found ivermectin did **not** reduce hospitalization or emergency observation for COVID-19 (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2207995).
- The **ACTIV-6 trial** (JAMA, 2022), a large U.S. trial, similarly found ivermectin did not meaningfully shorten symptom duration or improve outcomes compared to placebo (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2801827).

**Health authorities have concluded there's no benefit.** Based on the totality of evidence, the WHO updated its guidelines in November 2023 to **strongly recommend against** ivermectin for COVID-19, citing lack of evidence and biological plausibility (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic).

**Bottom line:** While early, weaker studies suggested a mortality benefit, this was not confirmed—and was effectively refuted—by larger, more rigorous randomized trials. The current scientific consensus is that ivermectin does **not** reduce COVID-19 mortality. Your sister's belief stems from outdated or lower-quality evidence that hasn't survived stronger scientific scrutiny.
